title: Genomic Changes and Critical Interactions Between Regulatory Cancer Stem Cell Lines and Intratumoral Somatic Lineages
content: In previous cancer research, cancer stem cells (CSCs) have generally been defined as undifferentiated, whereas somatic bulk tumor cells —by analogy with the somatic cells of the human body—have been considered differentiated and, in some contexts, referred to as non-stem cells. However, somatic cancer cells are not differentiated progeny generated through asymmetric cell division of self-renewing CSCs. Rather, they arise through cellular plasticity and mesenchymal-to-epithelial transition (MET) from CSCs, whereas new CSC clones and sublines can arise through the opposing epithelial-to-mesenchymal transition (EMT). These processes therefore do not represent conventional differentiation and dedifferentiation, but rather an ancestral form of “germ-to-soma” and “soma-to-germ” conversion that may serve to maintain proliferation and survival in unicellular systems or, in cancer, to enable continuous adaptation to microenvironmental and therapeutic stress. The hypoxic CSC-stemgermline that coordinates the cancer-cell life cycle is continuously challenged and damaged by the hyperoxic microenvironment and by the excessively high oxygen levels encountered in blood and tissue, particularly above 6.0% oxygen. Irreversibly damaged stemgermline DNA must therefore be rapidly repaired or replaced. Dysfunctional stemgermlines are continuously replaced by functional “replacement clones” generated from somatic tumor cells or revitalized through hyperpolyploid DNA-damage-response mechanisms involving genome reconstruction. Following conversion, oxygen-resistant somatic cancer cells protect the stemgermline genome and may therefore function as a virtually unlimited genomic reservoir for the generation of new stemgermlines and CSC clones. The large spectrum of intermediate and transient phenotypes arising during both conversion processes contributes to the intratumoral heterogeneity characteristic of cancer cell populations.
